x: Dhanananda was the last ruler of the Nanda dynasty of Magadha and was the Magadhan king at the time of Alexander's invasion. The Mauryas replaced the Nandas.
t: Link the ruler to his dynasty.

x: This item is doubtful: all four statements are true. Dhanananda was called Agrammes by the Greeks, Porus is Puru, Ambhi of Taxila supported Alexander and Bhaddasala was Dhanananda's commander. The key marks the Ambhi statement.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Porus lost at the Hydaspes (Jhelum), yet the battle's location is not why Alexander restored his kingdom; it was restored as an ally.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: I, II and III are correct: political disunity, a superior army and Indian allies helped Alexander. IV is false because Chandragupta never defeated Alexander.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: I, II and III are correct: Porus (Puru) ruled between the Jhelum and Chenab and had his kingdom restored. IV is false because Dhanananda, not Porus, was the Magadha ruler.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: I, II and III are correct: Alexander invaded in 326 BC, left in 325 BC and returned via Patala (Paatal). IV is false because Chandragupta did not defeat Alexander.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Dhanananda was the Magadha ruler, Bhaddasala his commander, Agrammes his Greek name and Ambhi the Indian ruler who supported Alexander, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each person.

x: Alexander fought Porus at the Jhelum, the Chenab bounded Porus's territory, Massaga was the Ashvaka capital and Paatal was the return point, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each place.

x: Three are reasons for Alexander's success: political disunity, a superior army and Indian allies. Restoration of Porus's kingdom was a result of the war, not a reason.
t: Separate causes of success from outcomes.

x: Massaga was the capital of the Ashvakas (Assakenoi), where Alexander faced stiff resistance. Jhelum and Chenab are rivers and Paatal was his return point.
t: Link the republic to its capital.

x: About 28 independent powers existed in north-west India at the time of Alexander's campaign, and this disunity helped him.
t: Recall the number of powers cited.

x: After his defeat Porus not only had his kingdom restored but also received additional territory from Alexander. The other options describe other people.
t: Recall what happened to Porus after the battle.

x: At Massaga, women took up arms and joined the resistance against Alexander after the men fell.
t: Recall the resistance at Massaga.

x: Pushyamitra Shunga, commander of the last Mauryan king Brihadratha, killed him and founded the Shunga dynasty. Vasudeva Kanva founded the Kanvas; Agnimitra and Devabhuti were later Shungas.
t: Identify the founder of the dynasty.

x: Pushyamitra Shunga killed Brihadratha in about 185 BCE, ending Mauryan rule and starting the Shunga dynasty.
t: Recall the year the Mauryan rule ended.

x: The Shungas ruled from about 185 BCE, when Brihadratha was killed, to about 73 BCE, when Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti.
t: Recall the start and end dates of Shunga rule.

x: Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra, ruled from Vidisha and is the hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram.
t: Link Agnimitra to his seat of rule.

x: Pushyamitra Shunga was a Brahmin; the Kanvas who followed the Shungas were also Brahmins.
t: Recall the varna of the Shunga founder.

x: Option C is incorrect: Pushyamitra performed two, not three, Ashwamedha yajnas. The Ayodhya inscription records the two sacrifices, and Patanjali is linked with them.
t: Check the number in each statement.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Patanjali lived in the Shunga period and supervised Pushyamitra's Ashwamedha ceremonies, which shows they were contemporaries.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Agnimitra being the hero does not by itself explain that the play is about his love for Malavika.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Vasudeva Kanva killed the last Shunga king Devabhuti and founded the Kanva dynasty, which is how the Kanvas succeeded the Shungas.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: the Shunga ancestors are said to come from Ujjain, and Agnimitra ruled from Vidisha.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All four are correct: Kalidasa wrote Malavikagnimitram as his first play, and its hero Agnimitra was the son of Pushyamitra Shunga.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Malavikagnimitram is by Kalidasa, Mahabhashya by Patanjali, Mrichchhakatikam by Sudraka, and Malavika is the heroine loved by Agnimitra, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the author of each work.

x: Brihadratha was the last Mauryan, Pushyamitra founded the Shungas, Devabhuti was the last Shunga and Vasudeva Kanva was the minister who killed him, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each ruler.

x: The Mauryas (322-185 BCE) were followed by the Shungas (185-73 BCE), the Kanvas (73-28 BCE) and then the Kushans (1st century CE), giving B, D, A, C.
t: Arrange the dynasties by period.

x: Three are correct: Pushyamitra was a Brahmin, the Shunga ancestors came from Ujjain and Patanjali wrote Mahabhashya. Statement 4 is false because Devabhuti was the last Shunga, not the founder.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Magadha was the core region of the Shungas, who took over the Mauryan heartland. Vidisha is Agnimitra's seat, Ujjain the ancestral home and Ayodhya the inscription site.
t: Discriminate the core region from linked places.

x: Darius I of Persia (Achaemenid) was the first foreign ruler to invade parts of north-west India, around 518 BCE, before Alexander.
t: Recall the earliest invader.

x: Option C is incorrect: Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 712 CE, not North India. Alexander beat Porus at the Jhelum, Skandagupta repelled the Hunas and Chandragupta II defeated the Sakas.
t: Check the region in each statement.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Porus being Alexander's opponent does not explain why Alexander won at the Jhelum.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Darius I invaded NW India, Alexander fought Porus, the Sakas ruled western India and the Hunas attacked the Gupta Empire, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the target of each invader.

x: All four are correct: the Indo-Greeks popularised gold coins in NW India, the Kushanas used gold and copper, Vima Kadphises issued gold coins for regular use, and the Saka-Kshatrapas used silver and copper.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Kanishka's coins show the Buddha, Mahmud Ghazni issued silver coins with Arabic and Sanskrit legends, Muhammad Ghori's coins bore Lakshmi and some the Kalma, and Chandragupta II issued silver Rupakas after beating the Sakas, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the coin feature of each ruler.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Hunas attacking in the Gupta period only gives the timing; it does not explain why Skandagupta resisted them.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Toramana led the second Huna attack and his son Mihirakula followed. Skandagupta had repelled the first attack, and Yashodharman later defeated Mihirakula.
t: Discriminate the Huna leaders.

x: Muhammad bin Qasim made the Arab conquest of Sindh, Mahmud Ghazni made 17 raids, Muhammad Ghori fought at Tarain and Chandawar, and Timur invaded Delhi in 1398, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the event linked to each invader.

x: Alexander came in 326 BCE, the Kushanas in the 1st century CE, the Hunas in the 5th century CE and Muhammad bin Qasim in 712 CE, giving D, C, A, B.
t: Arrange the invasions by century.

x: Muhammad Ghori fought Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1191, 1192) and defeated Jayachandra at Chandawar (1194). Panipat and Karnal belong to later invaders.
t: Recall the battles of Muhammad Ghori.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: being a Mongol invader does not explain why Genghis Khan reached the Indus in Iltutmish's time, chasing Jalaluddin Mangbarni.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526, Nadir Shah won at Karnal in 1739 and Abdali won the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.
t: Check each date and place.

x: Babur won at Panipat in 1526, Nadir Shah at Karnal in 1739, Ahmad Shah Abdali at Panipat in 1761 and Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the place and year of each invasion.

x: All four are correct: Kanishka's coins show the Buddha, Mahmud Ghazni issued bilingual Arabic-Sanskrit silver coins, Muhammad Ghori's coins bore Lakshmi and some the Kalma, and Strato II issued lead coins.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true: Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 712 CE, and Mahmud Ghazni made 17 raids between 1000 and 1027 CE.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman, Mahmud Ghazni plundered North India, Nadir Shah sacked Delhi and Ahmad Shah Abdali fought the Marathas, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the opponent or act of each invader.

x: Mihirakula attacked India, Muhammad bin Qasim defeated Dahir of Sindh, Genghis Khan reached the north-western frontier and Nadir Shah attacked Mughal India, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the target of each invader.

x: Darius I, the Achaemenid Persian king who first invaded north-west India, ruled from about 522 to 486 BCE. 326 BCE is Alexander's invasion.
t: Recall the reign period of Darius I.

x: Both are true: Alexander comes second in the list of invaders, after Darius I, and his campaign covered Punjab and north-western India.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Sakas are called Scythians because of their Central Asian origin, not because they came in the 1st century BCE.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Kanishka being a Kushana ruler does not explain why the Kushanas targeted north-western India.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Ghori's campaigns laying the foundation of Turkish rule is a result; it does not explain why his invasions began around 1175 CE.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Genghis Khan came in the 13th century, Timur invaded under Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughlaq, Babur founded the Mughal Empire and Abdali's invasions began in 1748, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the period of each invader.

x: The Mauryas were followed by the Shungas (185 BCE), the Kanvas (73 BCE) and then the Kushanas (1st century CE), giving A, B, C, D.
t: Arrange the dynasties by period.

x: Vima Kadphises took the title Sarvalokeshvara, Kujula Kadphises issued copper coins, Kanishka I put the Buddha on coins and Patanjali wrote Mahabhashya, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the feature of each person.

x: Option B is incorrect: the title Sarvalokeshvara, meaning Lord of the Whole World, was taken by Vima Kadphises, not Kanishka I. The other statements are right.
t: Discriminate Vima Kadphises from Kanishka.

x: All four are correct: Vima Kadphises was the first Kushana to issue gold coins, on a large scale and for regular use, while Kujula Kadphises issued copper coins.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true: the Indo-Greeks began gold-coin circulation in north-western India, and the Kushanas spread gold and copper coins on a wider scale.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Option A is correct: Chinese texts call Kanishka's people Yue-chi; after a Han princess was refused to him, the Kushanas marched against Pan Chao in 86 AD and lost to a smaller Chinese force.
t: Check each detail of the account.

x: Kushana trade with the Roman world ran through the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea.
t: Recall the sea route of Kushana trade.

x: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes ports of the period, and excavations at Arikamedu, a Roman trading post, confirm them. The other sources are not about ports.
t: Link the source to trade evidence.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Greek and Indo-Greek influence describes the Gandhara style; it does not explain why the school flourished under the Kushanas, which was due to their patronage.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Two are Kushana schools: Gandhara and Mathura. Sarnath is a Gupta-period style and Amaravati is linked with the Satavahanas.
t: Discriminate Kushana schools from others.

x: Kanishka patronised the Fourth Buddhist Council, held at Kundalvana in Kashmir, with Vasumitra as president and Ashvaghosha as vice-president, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each in the council.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: R describes Mahayana beliefs; it does not explain why the council led to the Hinayana-Mahayana split.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Three were at Kanishka's court: Parshva, Nagarjuna and Charaka. Patanjali belonged to the earlier Shunga period.
t: Discriminate Kushana scholars from Shunga ones.

x: Ashvaghosha was Kanishka's poet laureate, Vasumitra headed the Fourth Council, Charaka was court physician and Patanjali wrote Mahabhashya, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each scholar.

x: Both are true: the Sarnath Buddha image inscription is dated 81 AD, three years after Kanishka's accession in 78 AD.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Option C is correct: many historians credit Kanishka with starting the Saka era in 78 AD, the year of his accession. It is not 81 AD, nor linked to Vima Kadphises.
t: Recall the start year of the Saka era.

x: The Vikrama era starts in 57 BCE and the Saka era in 78 CE, so they differ by 135 years.
t: Add the two era start years.

x: The Rabatak inscription was found near Surkh Kotal in Afghanistan in 1993; it uses the Greek script and the Bactrian language, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall each detail of the inscription.

x: Yaudheya copper coins show the six-headed Kartikeya with a peacock, his mount.
t: Recall the deity on Yaudheya coins.

x: The Kushanas ruled roughly from the 1st to the 3rd century CE, with Kanishka's accession in 78 CE.
t: Recall the Kushana period.

x: The Greeks came in 326 BCE, the Sakas in the 1st century BCE and the Kushanas in the 1st century CE, giving A, B, C.
t: Arrange the invaders by century.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the flourishing of the Gandhara school under the Kushanas is a result of patronage; it does not explain why Kanishka supported it.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All three are correct: Saundarananda, Buddhacharita and Sariputraprakarana are works of Ashvaghosha.
t: Recall the works of Ashvaghosha.

x: The Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka met in Kashmir in the 1st century AD.
t: Recall the century of the council.

x: Ashvaghosha wrote Saundarananda, the Rabatak inscription is of Kanishka, the Yaudheyas appear in the Puranas and Ashtadhyayi, and Kujula Kadphises issued copper coins, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the link for each item.

x: All four are correct: the Rabatak inscription says Kanishka's rule reached Saketa, Kaushambi, Pataliputra and Sri Champa.
t: Recall the cities named in the inscription.

x: This item is doubtful: the Manusmriti calls Shakas and similar foreign groups fallen Kshatriyas, but the Pratiharas arose centuries later, so all four is historically doubtful. The key gives all four.
t: Check each group against the text's period.

x: The Kushana Empire was ruled by the Kushana dynasty and stretched beyond India into Central Asia and Afghanistan. Kanvas, Shungas and Mauryas are different dynasties.
t: Link the empire to its dynasty and extent.

x: All three are correct: Kanishka I was the greatest Kushana ruler, and the Rabatak inscription names Vima Kadphises as his father.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Vasumitra was a Buddhist scholar who presided over the Fourth Council. Charaka was the physician, Ashvaghosha the poet laureate and Patanjali the author of Mahabhashya.
t: Discriminate the scholars of the period.
